findings.title: Stale denial-cache entry overrides fresher permission data already in the server's cache
findings.body: In Service.Check, the permission-denial cache is consulted first and short-circuits the request, before the permission cache is checked for an allow. A denial entry is written only after a fresh DB lookup denies, but it then lives for shortCacheTTL (30s). Meanwhile, any DB re-query for the same user+action (triggered by a check on a different resource, or by cache expiry) rewrites the entire permCache scope map with fresh permissions, because getUserPermissions always calls permCache.Set after fetching. Concrete sequence: t0 Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) denies and caches a denial for dash1; t1 the user is granted access to dash1 and dash2; t2 Check(user, dashboards:read, dash2) misses the cached scope map, re-queries the DB, allows, and repopulates permCache with permissions that now include dash1; t3 Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) hits the stale denial entry and returns Allowed=false even though the server's own permission cache (and the DB) would allow it. The user stays denied for that resource until the denial entry expires. This partially undermines the PR's stated goal (a single check that races the permission write poisons the resource for 30s). Checking the permission cache for an allow before consulting the denial cache would preserve the fast-deny path while preventing stale denials from overriding fresher allow data the server already holds.

findings.title: Denial-cache precedence test uses a non-allowing cache entry, so it passes even without the denial-cache code
findings.body: The subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" says it seeds the permission cache to "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but it actually sets s.permCache to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} — a value that does not grant the scope. With that value, checkPermission also denies via the normal cached path, and the subsequent DB fallback against the fake store (which has no permissions) denies as well, so assert.False(t, resp.Allowed) passes even if the entire permDenialCache branch in Service.Check were deleted. The comment contradicts the code, and the new denial-cache behavior — including the permDenialCache.Set after a DB denial in service.go — is effectively untested. Seed the cache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} so the test fails if the denial-cache check is removed or bypassed.
